deep_why: HyperDetector detects coordinated cyberattacks by tracking how multiple entities (processes, files, users) interact simultaneously. The core insight is that normal system events involve one-to-one relationships, while sophisticated attacks involve many entities acting together in single operations. By representing these as hyperedges—single connections that link multiple entities at once—the system naturally captures collaboration patterns an attacker would need. The mathematical guarantee comes from a foundational principle: if you represent relationships honestly (many-to-many when they exist), you preserve structural information that binary edges destroy. The attack detection then works because it can identify clusters of multi-entity events linked across time, which normal operations rarely exhibit. This honest representation, combined with attention mechanisms spanning distant regions of the interaction record, lets defenders spot the telltale signs of distributed attack stages that would be invisible in simpler models.

SEP-Attack generates adversarial text by creating an ensemble of surrogate models, then choosing which words to modify based on how transferable the resulting attack would be to the target system. The soundness rests on a mathematical fact: when you have multiple imperfect copies of a system, their disagreements reveal what patterns are brittle. By weighting those copies according to how well their vulnerabilities transfer (using a principled diversity measure), the method learns which word changes actually exploit the victim model rather than just fooling the surrogates. The method works because transferability follows a signal that can be estimated from the ensemble—if a word modification breaks multiple models in consistent ways, it likely breaks the target too. This probabilistic reasoning about the shared vulnerability structure is far more reliable than treating all surrogate models equally.

Noise-aware Coreset Selection shrinks massive recommendation datasets to small, representative subsets by finding samples that contribute most to learning while ignoring noisy labels. The core idea is that training should focus on high-quality examples, but identifying them is hard when data is corrupted. The method selects samples based on their contribution to the learning objective (measured through gradients), which is mathematically sound because samples that most influence the final model are the ones most worth keeping. Simultaneously, it refines the selection by removing low-confidence predictions—examples the model itself doubts—which are likely mislabeled. This two-stage approach works because it separates the problem: first preserve important signal (gradient-based selection), then filter obvious noise (uncertainty filtering). The result is a compact dataset that trains nearly as well as the full set despite being a fraction of the size.

OpenDigger assesses open source community health by computing statistical and network-based metrics from collaboration records. The soundness comes from a simple principle: sustained collaboration leaves measurable traces—how quickly issues are answered, how developers connect across projects, how repositories grow—and these traces correlate with community viability. The method works because it collects multi-dimensional data (response times, network structure, growth rates) rather than single metrics, which means it captures different aspects of health. A community might have slow issue response but strong interconnection, or vice versa; only by measuring both can you detect real health. The framework's value lies in providing customizable, fine-grained data collection that lets researchers design their own health indicators rather than relying on one-size-fits-all summaries.

ONE-PASS accelerates ranking by approximating the full decision tree of possible orderings using a single forward computation. The mathematical trick is recognizing that ranking permutations (which explode factorially) can be reduced to subset combinations (which only double in count), because language models deciding the next item care less about the exact order of preceding items than about which items are present. The method further breaks the full ranking into smaller sub-rankings, then reassembles their probabilities using a principled inversion formula that recovers the contribution of each subset. This works because the inversion formula is mathematically exact—it correctly decomposes how subsets combine into the full ranking. By reducing the search space from factorial scale to subset scale and aggregating carefully, the system approximates auto-regressive ranking in one shot, eliminating the latency of decoding token by token.

This framework enables private authentication by proving knowledge of a secret without revealing it, using cryptographic techniques based on the discrete logarithm problem. The soundness comes from a deep mathematical guarantee: the discrete logarithm is computationally hard, meaning if someone can prove they know it (via the Schnorr protocol), they must truly know it—they cannot fake that knowledge. A zero-knowledge proof adds another layer: the proof itself leaks no information about the secret beyond its existence. The system works because it replaces the vulnerable centralized model (where a server stores all secrets and becomes a breach target) with mathematics: authentication happens through proofs that neither party learns anything exploitable, relying only on computational hardness that holds against all known attacks.

PrivSniffer detects implicit privacy leaks in text by building a graph where words connect based on semantic meaning, then searching for chains of inferences that reveal sensitive information. The core principle is that privacy breaches often work through implication—a single sentence might be harmless, but read alongside context clues elsewhere in the text, it exposes personal details. By modeling these clues as a graph and using language model reasoning to trace inference paths, the system uncovers what would be inferred by an attacker combining multiple pieces. The method is sound because it automates the adversarial reasoning: if the system can find an inference path, so can a malicious data collector. Combining graph search precision with language model inference power catches both obvious leaks and subtle contextual ones.

Temporal-Series-Aware Positional Encoding improves recommendation systems by encoding the timing intervals between user actions rather than absolute positions. The insight is that time gaps reveal emotional intensity—long waits suggest user hesitation or deliberation, while quick clicks show engagement. Instead of treating intervals as fixed numbers, the method encodes their sequence structure (whether gaps are lengthening, shortening, or stable), which captures behavioral trends more faithfully. This works because a sequence of time intervals is itself a signal about user state, and modeling that sequence through convolutional and attention mechanisms extracts meaningful patterns. By combining this temporal sequence information with traditional positional encoding, the system captures both what items a user viewed and the emotional arc of their interaction, improving prediction of future interest.

EC-spLLM trains specialized language models by selectively combining internal model knowledge with expert-provided answers, using hallucination detection to decide which source to trust. The core principle is that some problems are answered best by the language model's existing knowledge, while others require external expertise—the key is knowing which is which. By detecting when the model's self-generated answers are unreliable (hallucination detection), the system can confidently adopt expert answers in those cases and use model-generated answers when the model is confident. This bootstrapping works because the hallucination detector itself learns from both sources, creating a feedback loop where the growing dataset of high-quality answers improves both the model and the knowledge graph. Over iterations, the system converges toward a synergy where neither source dominates—expert knowledge fills gaps while model knowledge provides reliable background.

SecureSplit defends split learning (collaborative training) against backdoor attacks by transforming poisoned embeddings to make them visually distinct, then filtering them out via majority voting. The principle is that malicious participants subtly alter their embeddings to embed hidden attack triggers, but these alterations leave detectable fingerprints. By applying a dimensionality transformation that amplifies the difference between clean and poisoned embeddings, the system makes backdoors visible. Once visible, a simple voting scheme removes the poisoned examples while keeping the majority of clean ones. This works because backdoor attacks must be subtle (to avoid detection during normal training), which means they affect only a fraction of embeddings. When you amplify the subtle differences and use majority voting, the clean data naturally dominates and removes the contamination.

This workshop abstract addresses emerging foundations for AI agents operating autonomously on the web, touching on interoperability, protocols, reputation, and governance. The core principle is that for agents to coordinate at scale (billions operating independently), they need shared standards for communication, trustworthiness assessment, and conflict resolution—much like how the web itself runs on agreed-upon protocols. Without these foundations, agents either operate in isolation or risk malicious misuse. The workshop's value is examining what architectural and economic mechanisms (reputation systems, accountability frameworks, governance rules) would let diverse, autonomous agents act as first-class web entities without centralized control, while remaining robust to adversarial behavior.

DynaFLUX maximizes influence spread in networks where the topology is hidden or noisy by learning latent dynamics directly from time series data of node activations. The method is sound because it inverts the causality inference: instead of observing the network structure and predicting cascades, it observes cascade patterns over time and infers the underlying structure. By modeling nodes as interacting dynamical systems, the system captures how one node's activation affects others' future behavior, which implicitly reconstructs the influence graph. Reinforcement learning then optimizes seed selection using this learned model as reward signal. This works because time series of activations contain enough information to recover influence relationships—dense connections show up as synchronized activity, while weak links show as delayed or intermittent effects.

This work predicts when web searchers experience cognitive surprise by analyzing eye-movement patterns. The core insight is that expectancy violations manifest in how long and often people look at content, not in where they initially look. The method is sound because eye engagement time reflects conscious processing—when content surprises you, you stare longer trying to reconcile the mismatch. Initial attention (where you look first) is automatic and driven by visual features; sustained attention reflects active sense-making. By training on the temporal properties of gaze (total duration, fixation count), the system learns to detect the processing effort that distinguishes surprise from mere attention. This lets adaptive interfaces detect cognitive mismatches in real-time and respond with clarification or reformatting.

Make It Long, Keep It Fast scales sequence recommendation to 10,000-item histories by replacing expensive self-attention (where every item attends to every other) with target-to-history cross-attention (where the next-item prediction attends to history), reducing quadratic cost to linear. The method works because sequence self-attention computes relationships between all pairs of items, which is wasteful for ranking—you really need to ask which past items are relevant to the current choice. By inverting attention direction, the system focuses computation on the few relevant comparisons. Further, by batching multiple targets from the same user and sharing their history encoding, the system avoids redundant computation. Length-extrapolative training (training on shorter windows, testing on longer ones) succeeds because the attention mechanism naturally generalizes—attending to more items follows the same pattern as attending to fewer.

D2Map infers road networks from vehicle trajectories by combining two complementary views: rasterized images (showing density) and trajectory sequences (showing traversability). The principle is that a single representation loses information—density images miss adjacency between roads at different levels, while trajectory sequences alone miss global structure. By modeling both the rasterized view (what was driven) and the primal-dual graph structure (which roads are adjacent, which are separate), the system captures road relationships that neither representation alone provides. The strategy-adaptive fusion decides which representation is most reliable for each region based on local data patterns. This dual-view approach is sound because it treats each view as contributing partial but complementary evidence about the true road structure, and evidence fusion (rather than choosing one view) recovers more accurate topology.
